extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers, students of improvisational theatre, and readers interested in Mick Napier's approach
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for creating, directing, and performing improvised scenes following Mick Napier's revisionist improv theory. Focuses on why scenes work or fail, reappraising rules, actor behavior, scene context, and exercises for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question many of the accepted rules of the artform
rubrics_metrics.description: Napier's work 'attempts to question many of the accepted rules of the artform' and is described as a 'revisionist' theory on improvisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach rules skeptically: examine their origins and whether they are corrective band-aids for bad habits rather than universal truths. Use this questioning to re-evaluate commonly taught practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles on why and how scenes work or don't work
rubrics_metrics.description: The book 'discusses principles on why and how scenes work or don't work,' analyzing the mechanics behind successful and failed scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate scenes by tracing causal factors (choices, offers, relationships, energy) rather than relying solely on prescriptive rules; diagnose root causes of failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge the canon of improv conventional wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Napier 'challeng[es] the canon of improv conventional wisdom' and examines what's behind conventional instructions and how they came to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching or critiquing, contrast conventional wisdom with observed scene outcomes; prefer empirical, practice-based reasoning over dogma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismiss traditional improv instructions where counterproductive
rubrics_metrics.description: The book 'dismisses these traditional improv instructions,' implying some standard teachings should be set aside when they stem from a corrective, fearful mindset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify instructions that encourage over-analysis or fear; replace them with techniques that promote presence, clarity, and organic scene development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question the philosophy of 'Yes, And'
rubrics_metrics.description: Napier goes 'so far as to question the philosophy of Yes, And, and provides his own advice in their place.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat 'Yes, And' as an unquestionable axiom — assess when affirmation is useful and when alternative responses or constraints better serve a scene's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Perfect Actor (model/ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The book 'features an updated version of his The Perfect Actor essay.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'Perfect Actor' concept as a performance benchmark: consider qualities Napier emphasizes (implicit in the essay) when evaluating actors — e.g., presence, risk-taking, clarity of choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules (chapter)
rubrics_metrics.description: One chapter is titled 'Rules' — a focused treatment of rules governing improv practice (and Napier's reappraisal of them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study which rules are described, their intended corrective function, and Napier's critiques; apply or discard rules based on whether they improve scene outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Improvise (practical technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: A chapter called 'How to Improvise' provides practical instruction on improvisational methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess performers by their execution of practical techniques presented (offers, beats, beats progression, listening, status work) as described in the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: What About My Partner? (partner dynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: A chapter titled '"What About My Partner?"' focuses on relationships and interaction between scene partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate attention to partners: responsiveness, support, leadership/followership balance, and how choices affect partner play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and Scenes (contextual awareness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A chapter titled 'Context and Scenes' addresses the role of context in scene work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge scenes on how well context is established and used to generate meaningful choices, how context directs character relationships and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common Problems (diagnosis and correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A chapter called 'Common Problems' catalogs frequent scene issues and their causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the identified common problems as a diagnostic checklist when critiquing scenes; prioritize root-cause fixes rather than surface-level admonitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: More Than Two People in a Scene (ensemble management)
rubrics_metrics.description: A chapter titled 'More Than Two People in a Scene' treats dynamics specific to scenes with larger ensembles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well performers manage focus, clarity of relationships, and distribution of offers in multi-player scenes to avoid chaos and ensure narrative progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advanced Improvisation (higher-level techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: A chapter named 'Advanced Improvisation' covers techniques for more experienced improvisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess mastery of complex strategies (e.g., layered offers, thematic play, long-form architecture) and appropriate risk-taking consistent with advanced practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice and Guidelines for Improvisers (practical recommendations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A chapter called 'Advice and Guidelines for Improvisers' provides concrete recommendations for performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these guidelines as behavioral and strategic criteria when coaching or evaluating improvisers (warmups, habits, rehearsal practices, onstage decision-making).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvisation and the Second Law of Thermodynamics (conceptual framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A chapter titled 'Improvisation and the Second Law of Thermodynamics' links improv concepts to a physical/energetic metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the energy/entropy metaphor to evaluate scene momentum, escalation/decay of ideas, and how performers inject or conserve 'energy' to sustain interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises to Do at Home (practice and skill-building)
rubrics_metrics.description: A chapter 'Exercises to Do at Home' offers exercises for individual practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure commitment and skill development by use of recommended exercises; use exercise completion and improvement as metrics for progress.
